dharana.numbering_edition: Jaideva Singh 1979 (dhāraṇā 1 = verse 24; dhāraṇā 82 = verses 105–106 and dhāraṇā 89 = verses 113–114, otherwise one verse each; dhāraṇā 112 = verse 137)
dharana.sanskrit_iast: madhyajihve sphāritāsye madhye nikṣipya cetanām | hoccāraṃ manasā kurvaṃs tataḥ śānte pralīyate ||
dharana.sanskrit_source: GRETIL e-text, compared with Wallis's concordance, Pradīpaka and the Singh scan
dharana.rendering: With the mouth wide open and the tongue in the middle, placing awareness in the middle, and sounding 'ha' in the mind, one dissolves into peace.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh reads the tongue as inverted against the palate (khecarī mudrā, as described in the Vivekamārtaṇḍa) and explains: the breath naturally sounds haṃsa; with the tongue inverted the 's' cannot form and only 'ha' remains, a vowel-less 'ha' that can only be sounded mentally, and repeating it develops the middle state. Wallis and Bäumer read 'the tongue in the middle of the wide open mouth'; Wallis adds 'pointing up'. This door follows the plain reading and does not teach tongue inversion.
dharana.instruction: Let the mouth fall open, rest the tongue in the middle, and silently sound 'ha'.

verification.notes: Door index = Singh dhāraṇā number, read directly in Singh's own headings and cross-checked against The Mystery Within's Singh-numbered list and Wallis's concordance. Caveat: Singh was read from an OCR scan, not a print copy in hand.

source_disagreements: Tongue: Singh reads the tongue inverted toward the palate (khecarī mudrā); Wallis and Bäumer read it resting in the middle of the open mouth. This door follows the latter.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 81 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

points: the tongue resting in the middle
the mental sound 'ha' in the middle of the open space
geometry.summary: Not a body shape. The map is the open space of the mouth, the tongue resting in its middle, and a silent 'ha' sounding in that space.
geometry.svg_hint: a soft open oval with a small mark at its centre and a faint 'ha' inside
geometry.honesty: Geometry records the dharana's own map of attention, not a body shape. Locations marked 'commentarial' come from commentary, not from the verse.

reaction.name: Silent 'ha'
reaction.summary: School metaphor only: a held jaw lets go, the mouth opens, and a silent sound dissolves into peace. Not a biochemical or medical claim.

breath.lands_in: the open mouth, as the mental 'ha' fades
breath.cue: Natural breath through the nose or the open mouth, whichever is comfortable. The 'ha' is silent, in the mind only. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

orientation.cue: Let the jaw drop and the mouth open; rest the tongue in the middle
orientation.gravity: Let the floor or chair carry the body completely; there is no posture to hold
orientation.degrees_hint: No angle target: the VBT gives no posture for this dharana

attention.primary: The middle of the open mouth

adiyogi.verse_paraphrase: With the mouth wide open and the tongue in the middle, placing awareness in the middle, and sounding 'ha' in the mind, one dissolves into peace.
adiyogi.method_summary: Let the jaw relax so the mouth opens wide, without strain. Rest the tongue in the middle of the mouth. Place awareness in the middle of that open space and sound 'ha' silently, in the mind only. Let it dissolve into peace.

honesty.disclosure: Door 058 follows Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra dharana 58 (verse 81) in Jaideva Singh's numbering. The door-to-dharana index is a School of 112 Doorways teaching device. Singh's sequence is one edition's count, not an ancient one-to-one canon. The seat, counts, reaction and beat scripts are school additions.
honesty.notes: pairing_type is school_device: the dharana is the content, while the door index, seat and pacing are the school's.

safety.pain_rule: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.
safety.open_seat_alternate: This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.
safety.contraindication_notes: General practice caution only; not medical advice. Open the mouth only as wide as is comfortable; close it whenever the jaw tires. Tongue inversion is not taught. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
